payload.native_system_prompt:
You are part of an optimization system that improves a given text (i.e. the variable). You are the gradient (feedback) engine. Your only responsibility is to give intelligent and creative feedback and constructive criticism to variables, given an objective specified in <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> </OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION> tags. The variables may be solutions to problems, prompts to language models, code, or any other text-based variable. Pay attention to the role description of the variable, and the context in which it is used. You should assume that the variable will be used in a similar context in the future. Only provide strategies, explanations, and methods to change in the variable. DO NOT propose a new version of the variable, that will be the job of the optimizer. Your only job is to send feedback and criticism (compute 'gradients'). For instance, feedback can be in the form of 'Since language models have the X failure mode...', 'Adding X can fix this error because...', 'Removing X can improve the objective function because...', 'Changing X to Y would fix the mistake ...', that gets at the downstream objective.
If a variable is already working well (e.g. the objective function is perfect, an evaluation shows the response is accurate), you should not give feedback.

### Glossary of tags that will be sent to you:
# - <LM_SYSTEM_PROMPT>: The system prompt for the language model.
# - <LM_INPUT>: The input to the language model.
# - <LM_OUTPUT>: The output of the language model.
# - <OBJECTIVE_FUNCTION>: The objective of the optimization task.
# - <VARIABLE>: Specifies the span of the variable.
# - <ROLE>: The role description of the variable.
payload.instruction: Make this look like a comic book photo
payload.rubric: Judge requested image editing: yes means all requested changes are complete, no means no requested change has progressed, partial means some progress without complete fulfillment. Unrelated edits are not requested progress. Insufficient evidence stays unresolved.

node.question: Does the edited image retain recognizable photographic subject matter and appearance?
node.criteria: Pass if the edited image retains recognizable photographic subject matter and appearance; fail if it does not; unknown if the image evidence is insufficient.
node.binding: Assess the edited image for photographic subject matter and appearance. This observation describes the result and does not by itself establish progress toward the requested edit.

Make the criterion explicitly distinguish complete, partial, absent, and unresolved using the existing s1/s2/s3 evidence: comic-book treatment is the requested change, photographic appearance is the retained quality, and s2 alone is not progress. Preserve the current evidence-based absent judgment here: the edited street scene remains photographic with no visible comic-book treatment; framing/tonal differences do not establish progress. Do not treat the reference label as atomic ground truth or force “no.” Keep unresolved for genuinely insufficient visual evidence. The one unknown trace is a transport/SSL failure in s1, not negative visual evidence; ensure it remains unresolved rather than being converted to absent. Repeated high-confidence traces support the current criterion, so focus edits on clarifying the binding and outcome boundaries, not changing the visual threshold.
s3: Replace the truncated binding with a complete, direct comparison criterion that separates the requested comic-book treatment from the retained photographic quality. Make clear that visible progress toward comic-book styling counts even if incomplete, while retaining the scene as a photograph alone—or incidental framing or tonal differences—does not. Keep insufficient visual evidence unresolved; a transport or dependency failure is not evidence of absence. The repeated valid traces support the current absent judgment for these images, but treat that as visual evidence rather than as a conclusion dictated by the reference label. Avoid adding mandatory techniques or changing the visual threshold.
